v: Exodus 24:7 (KJV): “And he took the book of the covenant, and read in the audience of the people: and they said, All that the LORD hath said will we do, and be obedient.”

Moses read this book aloud at Mount Sinai and the people promised to obey it. Most scholars think it was a written collection of the laws now found in Exodus 20:22-23:33 (often called the 'Covenant Code'), so much of its content may survive inside Exodus, but the separate book itself is not preserved.
No copy of this book is known to survive. This is a reference entry, not an ancient text.

Numbers 21:14-15 (KJV): “Wherefore it is said in the book of the wars of the LORD, What he did in the Red sea, and in the brooks of Arnon, And at the stream of the brooks that goeth down to the dwelling of Ar, and lieth upon the border of Moab.”
Apparently an old collection of songs or poems about Israel's battles in the wilderness. Numbers quotes two lines of it about the valleys of Arnon. Nothing else survives.
No copy of this book is known to survive. This is a reference entry, not an ancient text.

Joshua 10:13 (KJV): “And the sun stood still, and the moon stayed, until the people had avenged themselves upon their enemies. Is not this written in the book of Jasher? So the sun stood still in the midst of heaven, and hasted not to go down about a whole day.”
2 Samuel 1:18 (KJV): “(Also he bade them teach the children of Judah the use of the bow: behold, it is written in the book of Jasher.)”

An early Israelite collection of poems or songs. The Bible quotes it for the sun standing still at Gibeon and for David's lament over Saul and Jonathan (the 'Song of the Bow'). Books printed later under the name 'Jasher' (a medieval Hebrew Sefer haYashar, an 18th-century English forgery, and the 1840 English translation of the Hebrew work) are not this ancient book.
No copy of this book is known to survive. This is a reference entry, not an ancient text.
1 Samuel 10:25 (KJV): “Then Samuel told the people the manner of the kingdom, and wrote it in a book, and laid it up before the LORD. And Samuel sent all the people away, every man to his house.”

Samuel wrote down 'the manner of the kingdom' (the rights and duties of the king) in a book and laid it up before the LORD when Saul became king. Its text is lost; compare Deuteronomy 17:14-20 and 1 Samuel 8:11-18.
No copy of this book is known to survive. This is a reference entry, not an ancient text.
1 Kings 11:41 (KJV): “¶ And the rest of the acts of Solomon, and all that he did, and his wisdom, are they not written in the book of the acts of Solomon?”
A record of Solomon's reign and wisdom that the writer of Kings used as a source. It has not survived.
No copy of this book is known to survive. This is a reference entry, not an ancient text.
1 Kings 14:19 (KJV): “And the rest of the acts of Jeroboam, how he warred, and how he reigned, behold, they are written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel.”
Royal annals of the northern kingdom, cited about 18 times in 1-2 Kings for 'the rest of the acts' of Israel's kings. Not the biblical books of Chronicles, which were written later. Lost.
No copy of this book is known to survive. This is a reference entry, not an ancient text.
1 Kings 14:29 (KJV): “¶ Now the rest of the acts of Rehoboam, and all that he did, are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah?”
Royal annals of the southern kingdom, cited about 15 times in 1-2 Kings. Not the biblical books of Chronicles. Lost.
No copy of this book is known to survive. This is a reference entry, not an ancient text.

1 Chronicles 29:29 (KJV): “Now the acts of David the king, first and last, behold, they are written in the book of Samuel the seer, and in the book of Nathan the prophet, and in the book of Gad the seer,”
One of three prophetic records of David's reign named by the Chronicler. Some think it means material now in 1-2 Samuel, but the book as cited is not preserved separately.
No copy of this book is known to survive. This is a reference entry, not an ancient text.

1 Chronicles 29:29 (KJV): “Now the acts of David the king, first and last, behold, they are written in the book of Samuel the seer, and in the book of Nathan the prophet, and in the book of Gad the seer,”

2 Chronicles 9:29 (KJV): “¶ Now the rest of the acts of Solomon, first and last, are they not written in the book of Nathan the prophet, and in the prophecy of Ahijah the Shilonite, and in the visions of Iddo the seer against Jeroboam the son of Nebat?”
A record by the prophet Nathan of the reigns of David and Solomon. Lost, though parts may lie behind the accounts in Samuel and Kings.
No copy of this book is known to survive. This is a reference entry, not an ancient text.

1 Chronicles 29:29 (KJV): “Now the acts of David the king, first and last, behold, they are written in the book of Samuel the seer, and in the book of Nathan the prophet, and in the book of Gad the seer,”
A record by David's seer Gad, cited with the books of Samuel and Nathan. Lost.
No copy of this book is known to survive. This is a reference entry, not an ancient text.

2 Chronicles 9:29 (KJV): “¶ Now the rest of the acts of Solomon, first and last, are they not written in the book of Nathan the prophet, and in the prophecy of Ahijah the Shilonite, and in the visions of Iddo the seer against Jeroboam the son of Nebat?”
Ahijah foretold that Jeroboam would rule ten tribes (1 Kings 11:29-39). His written prophecy, a source for Solomon's reign, is lost.
No copy of this book is known to survive. This is a reference entry, not an ancient text.

2 Chronicles 9:29 (KJV): “¶ Now the rest of the acts of Solomon, first and last, are they not written in the book of Nathan the prophet, and in the prophecy of Ahijah the Shilonite, and in the visions of Iddo the seer against Jeroboam the son of Nebat?”
Visions of the seer Iddo 'against Jeroboam the son of Nebat', cited as a source for Solomon's reign. Lost.
No copy of this book is known to survive. This is a reference entry, not an ancient text.

2 Chronicles 12:15 (KJV): “Now the acts of Rehoboam, first and last, are they not written in the book of Shemaiah the prophet, and of Iddo the seer concerning genealogies? And there were wars between Rehoboam and Jeroboam continually.”
A record of King Rehoboam's reign by the prophet Shemaiah (see 1 Kings 12:22-24), cited together with Iddo's genealogies. Lost.
No copy of this book is known to survive. This is a reference entry, not an ancient text.
2 Chronicles 13:22 (KJV): “And the rest of the acts of Abijah, and his ways, and his sayings, are written in the story of the prophet Iddo.”
The 'story' (Hebrew midrash) of Iddo about King Abijah. Lost.
No copy of this book is known to survive. This is a reference entry, not an ancient text.

2 Chronicles 20:34 (KJV): “Now the rest of the acts of Jehoshaphat, first and last, behold, they are written in the book of Jehu the son of Hanani, who is mentioned in the book of the kings of Israel.”
A record of King Jehoshaphat's reign by the prophet Jehu son of Hanani (see 1 Kings 16:1), said to be included in the book of the kings of Israel. Lost.
No copy of this book is known to survive. This is a reference entry, not an ancient text.
2 Chronicles 26:22 (KJV): “¶ Now the rest of the acts of Uzziah, first and last, did Isaiah the prophet, the son of Amoz, write.”
Isaiah the prophet wrote 'the rest of the acts of Uzziah'. This record is not the canonical Book of Isaiah and has not survived.
No copy of this book is known to survive. This is a reference entry, not an ancient text.

2 Chronicles 33:19 (KJV): “His prayer also, and how God was intreated of him, and all his sin, and his trespass, and the places wherein he built high places, and set up groves and graven images, before he was humbled: behold, they are written among the sayings of the seers.”

A record of King Manasseh's prayer and sins 'among the sayings of the seers' (Hebrew hozai, which some read as a prophet's name). Lost. The later Prayer of Manasseh (in Bibley's Apocrypha shelf) was written to fill this gap.
No copy of this book is known to survive. This is a reference entry, not an ancient text.

2 Chronicles 35:25 (KJV): “¶ And Jeremiah lamented for Josiah: and all the singing men and the singing women spake of Josiah in their lamentations to this day, and made them an ordinance in Israel: and, behold, they are written in the lamentations.”

Jeremiah's laments for the good king Josiah, killed in 609 BC, were 'written in the lamentations'. Most scholars do not think this means the canonical Book of Lamentations, which mourns Jerusalem's fall. Lost.
No copy of this book is known to survive. This is a reference entry, not an ancient text.
Esther 2:23 (KJV): “And when inquisition was made of the matter, it was found out; therefore they were both hanged on a tree: and it was written in the book of the chronicles before the king.”
Esther 6:1 (KJV): “On that night could not the king sleep, and he commanded to bring the book of records of the chronicles; and they were read before the king.”

The Persian royal records where Mordecai's rescue of the king was written down, and which the sleepless king had read to him. Also called 'the book of the chronicles of the kings of Media and Persia' (Esther 10:2). Lost.
No copy of this book is known to survive. This is a reference entry, not an ancient text.
1 Corinthians 5:9 (KJV): “I wrote unto you in an epistle not to company with fornicators:”

Before 1 Corinthians, Paul had written the church a letter telling them not to keep company with the sexually immoral. That letter is lost (some scholars think a fragment survives in 2 Corinthians 6:14-7:1). The later '3 Corinthians' in Bibley's shelf is a 2nd-century work, not this letter.
No copy of this book is known to survive. This is a reference entry, not an ancient text.

2 Corinthians 2:4 (KJV): “For out of much affliction and anguish of heart I wrote unto you with many tears; not that ye should be grieved, but that ye might know the love which I have more abundantly unto you.”
2 Corinthians 7:8 (KJV): “For though I made you sorry with a letter, I do not repent, though I did repent: for I perceive that the same epistle hath made you sorry, though it were but for a season.”
Paul wrote the Corinthians a painful letter 'with many tears' between 1 and 2 Corinthians. It is lost, unless (as some scholars think) part of it survives as 2 Corinthians 10-13.
No copy of this book is known to survive. This is a reference entry, not an ancient text.
Ephesians 3:3 (KJV): “How that by revelation he made known unto me the mystery; (as I wrote afore in few words,”

Paul says he 'wrote afore in few words'. Many interpreters think this refers back to Ephesians 1-2 in the same letter rather than to a lost letter, so whether a separate earlier letter ever existed is uncertain.
No copy of this book is known to survive. This is a reference entry, not an ancient text.
Colossians 4:16 (KJV): “And when this epistle is read among you, cause that it be read also in the church of the Laodiceans; and that ye likewise read the epistle from Laodicea.”

Paul told the Colossians to read 'the epistle from Laodicea'. That letter is lost, though some think it is our Ephesians. The Latin 'Epistle to the Laodiceans' (in Bibley's Lost gospels and acts shelf) is a later compilation of phrases from Paul's letters, not the original.
No copy of this book is known to survive. This is a reference entry, not an ancient text.

Jude 1:14-15 (KJV): “And Enoch also, the seventh from Adam, prophesied of these, saying, Behold, the Lord cometh with ten thousands of his saints, To execute judgment upon all, and to convince all that are ungodly among them of all their ungodly deeds which they have ungodly committed, and of all their hard speeches which ungodly sinners have spoken against him.”

Jude quotes a prophecy of 'Enoch, the seventh from Adam'. The quotation matches 1 Enoch 1:9, so this prophecy actually survives inside the Book of 1 Enoch (in Bibley's Other Jewish writings shelf). It is listed here because the Bible cites it as a separate source.
The separate prophecy as Jude knew it is not preserved on its own, but its words survive inside 1 Enoch 1:9. This is a reference entry.
Origen, Homilies on Luke 1; Jerome, Preface to the Commentary on Matthew

Basilides taught in Alexandria around AD 120-140. Origen says he 'dared to write a Gospel according to Basilides'. A few fragments of his commentary (the Exegetica, in 24 books) survive in Clement of Alexandria and Hegemonius, but nothing certain of the 'gospel'. M. R. James suspected such heresiarchs' 'Gospels' were really their treatises, nicknamed gospels.
No copy of this gospel is known to survive. This is a reference entry, not an ancient text.
Cerinthus (about AD 100) was remembered as an opponent of John the apostle. Epiphanius says his followers used only part of Matthew's Gospel. No separate gospel text survives.
No copy of this gospel is known to survive. This is a reference entry, not an ancient text.
Tertullian, Against Marcion, book 4; Epiphanius, Panarion 42; Irenaeus, Against Heresies 1.27

Marcion of Sinope (about AD 140) published an edited version of Luke, removing what conflicted with his belief that the God of the Old Testament was not the Father of Jesus. It is lost, but scholars have partly reconstructed it from Tertullian's and Epiphanius's refutations.
No copy of this gospel is known to survive. This is a reference entry, not an ancient text.
Jerome, Preface to the Commentary on Matthew; Epiphanius, Panarion 44

Apelles was a 2nd-century disciple of Marcion who later developed his own teaching. Jerome lists a gospel 'of Apelles' among heretical gospels. Nothing of it is known to survive; some lines of his 'Syllogisms' are quoted by Ambrose.
No copy of this gospel is known to survive. This is a reference entry, not an ancient text.

Bardaisan (Bardesanes, AD 154-222) was a Christian philosopher and hymn-writer at Edessa in Syria. A gospel connected with his name is mentioned only in later sources, and nothing of it survives. The one work that survives from his circle is the 'Book of the Laws of Countries', written by his pupil Philip.
No copy of this gospel is known to survive. This is a reference entry, not an ancient text.
Cologne Mani Codex; al-Biruni; Manichaean and anti-Manichaean writers

Mani (AD 216-276), founder of Manichaeism, wrote a 'Living' or 'Great' Gospel in 22 sections, one for each letter of the Aramaic alphabet. Only short quotations survive, mainly in the Greek Cologne Mani Codex and the Arabic writer al-Biruni.
No copy of this gospel is known to survive. This is a reference entry, not an ancient text.
Origen, Homilies on Luke 1; Eusebius, Church History 3.25.6; Clement of Alexandria, Stromata 2.9; 3.4; 7.13 ('Traditions of Matthias')

A gospel under the name of Matthias, the apostle chosen to replace Judas (Acts 1:26). Eusebius lists it among heretical books. Clement of Alexandria quotes a few sayings from 'Traditions of Matthias', which may be the same work.
No copy of this gospel is known to survive. This is a reference entry, not an ancient text.
Epiphanius says certain Gnostic groups produced 'a forged gospel which they call the Gospel of Perfection'. Nothing of it survives.
No copy of this gospel is known to survive. This is a reference entry, not an ancient text.
Epiphanius quotes one passage from a Gnostic 'Gospel of Eve', beginning 'I stood on a high mountain and saw a tall man and another, short...'. That quotation is all that survives.
No copy of this gospel is known to survive. This is a reference entry, not an ancient text.
A gospel of this name is known only from its title in later lists of heretical (probably Manichaean) books. No content is known.
No copy of this gospel is known to survive. This is a reference entry, not an ancient text.
Origen, Homilies on Luke 1; Jerome, Preface to the Commentary on Matthew

Origen names a gospel 'according to the Twelve' among the gospels the church rejected. Many scholars identify it with the gospel of the Ebionites quoted by Epiphanius (see Gospel of the Ebionites in the New Testament Apocrypha shelf), but this is uncertain.
No copy of this gospel is known to survive. This is a reference entry, not an ancient text.
The medieval Muslim scholar al-Biruni mentions a 'Gospel of the Seventy' ascribed to a man named Balamis, in use among Manichaeans. Nothing of it survives.
No copy of this gospel is known to survive. This is a reference entry, not an ancient text.

A 'Gospel under the name of Thaddaeus' is named in manuscripts of the Gelasian Decree's list of books not to be received. Its content is unknown. (The Acts of Thaddaeus, a different work, is in the New Testament Apocrypha shelf.)
No copy of this gospel is known to survive. This is a reference entry, not an ancient text.
Gelasian Decree (6th century); the Greek List of Sixty Books (7th century)

An ancient 'Gospel under the name of Barnabas' is named in these lists of rejected books; nothing of it survives. It is different from the Italian 'Gospel of Barnabas', a late 15th- or 16th-century forgery, and from the Epistle of Barnabas (in Bibley's Early church writings shelf).
No copy of this gospel is known to survive. This is a reference entry, not an ancient text.

A dualist book used by the Priscillianists in 4th-century Spain, probably Manichaean in origin. Orosius quotes the only surviving fragment, in which the Savior is questioned privately by his disciples.
No copy of this gospel is known to survive. This is a reference entry, not an ancient text.
